common_name: Howard Asper Camellia (Giant Medium Pink Peony-Form Reticulata Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Howard Asper is a cross of two reticulata cultivars bred in California and prized for its exceptionally large peony-form blooms.

directions: Howard Asper was raised near San Diego from a cross of two reticulata cultivars and first flowered in the early 1960s, going on to earn top hybrid honors from American camellia growers within a few years of its debut. Its loosely arranged, medium-pink peony-form flowers open extra-large, with soft yellow anthers set off against pale filaments, on a plant that grows noticeably faster and more spreading than many reticulata cultivars. Give it consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil and dappled shade with shelter from drying winter wind, since the broad limbs and heavy bloom load are easily damaged in an exposed site. Feed lightly after flowering finishes and prune only to shape at that time, as next year's buds form on the current season's new growth.

common_name: Harold L. Paige Camellia (Giant Scarlet Rose-Form Reticulata Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this japonica x reticulata hybrid pairs reticulata-scale flower size with sturdier, more cold-tolerant japonica growth.

directions: Harold L. Paige was raised in Oakland, California from a japonica-reticulata cross and did not bloom until its eighth year, but the wait produced an enormous, brilliant scarlet rose-form double flower with dozens of petals that helped it earn multiple hybrid awards from American camellia societies. It grows slowly at first, developing into an upright, eventually spreading small tree with substantial dark green foliage, and its late-season bloom extends the reticulata flowering display well past when most pure reticulata cultivars have finished. Plant it in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade and protect it from harsh afternoon sun. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer once flowering ends and limit pruning to shaping cuts made right after bloom.

common_name: William Hertrich Camellia (Giant Deep Cherry-Red Semi-Double Reticulata Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; William Hertrich is a seedling of the historic Lion Head reticulata noted for its heavy, irregular petal texture.

directions: William Hertrich, named for the longtime superintendent who built the botanical collections at San Marino's Huntington Gardens, is a seedling of the historic Lion Head reticulata and carries forward that parent's substantial flower size. Its very large semi-double blooms open deep cherry-red to pink, with broad, reflexed outer petals surrounding a looser cluster of smaller upright petals that mingle informally with the stamens, giving the flower a heavier, more textured look than smooth-petaled reticulata cultivars. The shrub is a steady grower that can reach small-tree proportions after a decade in the ground, flowering in midseason. Site it in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with shelter from winter wind, and prune only to shape right after bloom since buds set on the current year's growth.

common_name: Curtain Call Camellia (Giant Coral-Rose Ruffled Semi-Double Reticulata Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Curtain Call arose as a chance seedling at a Southern California nursery and is grown for its large, ruffled coral-pink blooms.

directions: Curtain Call turned up as an unplanned chance seedling at a well-known Altadena, California camellia nursery and was distinctive enough by its first bloom to warrant naming and registration. Its very large, ruffled semi-double flowers open a deep coral-rose with a bright boss of golden stamens at the center, giving each bloom a lively, informal texture rather than the flat, smooth form typical of many reticulata cultivars. The shrub grows in a relatively open, fast-spreading habit with lighter green foliage than most reticulata camellias, flowering in mid-to-late winter into spring. Grow it in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade sheltered from drying wind, feeding lightly after bloom and pruning only to shape at that time.

common_name: Trewithen Pink Camellia (Historic Wild-Collected Pink Reticulata Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Trewithen Pink was selected from wild Yunnan seed collected on an early twentieth-century plant-hunting expedition and grows into a large, tree-like specimen over time.

directions: Trewithen Pink traces back to wild reticulata seed gathered in Yunnan during an early twentieth-century British plant-hunting expedition to China and was later singled out and given a clonal name at the Cornwall garden that raised it, making it one of the direct links between present-day reticulata camellias and the species' native mountain populations. Its flowers are simpler and less fully double than showier hybrid cultivars, closer in form to the wild species, but still substantial in size and produced on a vigorous plant that becomes tree-like with age in a mild, sheltered garden. It grows more slowly to flowering size than many modern hybrids and rewards patience with an authentic, historic garden presence. Provide deep, humus-rich, acidic soil, dappled shade, and protection from cold wind and hard freezes, since it retains some of the tenderness of the species' Yunnan origins.
